title: AI-powered clones challenge Adobe and Microsoft, stoking ‘SaaSpocalypse’ fears
summary: AI-powered clones challenge traditional software subscriptions, sparking SaaSpocalypse fears
detailed: As free programs that mimic software (SW) like Photoshop and Excel using artificial intelligence (AI) keep emerging, the SW industry is grappling with a headache.
With advances in AI coding, a small number of developers have replicated products from large SW corporations in a short time.
The fact that these programs were developed in a short period using Anthropic's AI model "Claude Opus 5.5" is also drawing attention.
In the past, complex SW development required large teams and long timelines, but now a small group of developers can use AI to implement similar programs in a short period.
sentences: As free programs that mimic software (SW) like Photoshop and Excel using artificial intelligence (AI) keep emerging, the SW industry is grappling with a headache.
With advances in AI coding, a small number of developers have replicated products from large SW corporations in a short time.
They include "Photocraft," modeled after Photoshop, as well as "Lightcraft," "Vectorcraft," and "Filmcraft," which respectively mimic Lightroom, Illustrator, and Premiere Pro.
They notably implement a user interface (UI) similar to existing Adobe products, including the workspace, tool layout, and shortcuts.
The programs released by Artcraft have drawn major attention on GitHub and Reddit.
In particular, Photocraft took the No.
1 spot on the daily popularity ranking of GitTrend, a GitHub trend analysis site, on the 7th, a week after its release.
The fact that these programs were developed in a short period using Anthropic's AI model "Claude Opus 5.5" is also drawing attention.
Artcraft said it reimplemented Adobe's main programs in just a few weeks using Claude and the Rust programming language.
Artcraft later released free open-source programs that mimic the Microsoft (MS) Office suite as well.
They include "Gridcraft," "Deckcraft," and "Wordcraft," modeled after Excel, PowerPoint, and Word, respectively.
Wordcraft is also drawing attention, securing about 16,600 stars on GitHub.
The company said these programs were also built with Claude Opus 5.5 and Rust.
Artcraft said it has already implemented a large share of the functions of existing commercial SW.
By its own assessment, Photocraft implements about 76% of Photoshop's main features, with readiness for real work at around 45%.
Vectorcraft, Lightcraft, and Filmcraft have work readiness levels of 62%, 59%, and 56%, respectively, and the three MS Office replacement programs are also in the 50%–60% range.

The developers set a goal of raising Photocraft's functionality to a level 99% similar to Photoshop within a few months.
◇ "An alternative to a closed SW ecosystem" vs.

"Technical and security limits remain"
Users are divided between anticipation and concern.

Adobe has effectively become the standard in creative fields such as image editing and video production for decades, but high subscription fees and early termination charges have fueled dissatisfaction.
Against this backdrop, expectations have grown that these tools could be an alternative to Adobe's subscription-centric business model and closed ecosystem.
On the other hand, there are concerns about copyright infringement.
Artcraft claims it used a so-called "clean-room design," developing anew by analyzing features and behavior externally without using source code from existing commercial SW.
However, even if no source code was copied, the programs could still lead to copyright disputes because they closely mimic the screen layouts, tool placements, and icons of Adobe and MS products.
If the two corporations take legal action, it could disrupt project operations.
There are also technical limits before these tools can replace commercial SW in practice.
Photocraft remains in an early development stage, with professional editing features and file compatibility not yet sufficiently verified.
In particular, because it was developed in a short time using AI, observers say further verification is needed on code stability, security vulnerabilities, and file processing errors.
Industry watchers say the case shows that AI is lowering the technological barriers to entry that existing SW corporations have built.
In the past, complex SW development required large teams and long timelines, but now a small group of developers can use AI to implement similar programs in a short period.
As a result, concern over a "SaaSpocalypse," in which the business models of existing subscription SW corporations could be threatened, is resurfacing.
As AI lowers the threshold for SW development, there are expectations of changes to the technological advantages and market dominance of existing corporations.
